title: Mossy flagstone floor tiles
tests: Seamless terrain at 16×16 with an interchangeable variant: repetition, seams, value control and texture without noise.
brief: Draw two 16×16 floor tiles for a top-down dungeon game. `flagstone`: worn grey flagstones with moss growing in some of the joints. `flagstone-cracked`: the same stones with one slab cracked across.

Use only these 16 colours (the PICO-8 palette): #000000, #1d2b53, #7e2553, #008751, #ab5236, #5f574f, #c2c3c7, #fff1e8, #ff004d, #ffa300, #ffec27, #00e436, #29adff, #83769c, #ff77a8, #ffccaa, and at most 8 of them in each tile. Every pixel is fully opaque.

Each tile repeats seamlessly in both directions: no line doubles where tiles meet and nothing changes abruptly across the edge. Any cell of a floor of `flagstone` can be swapped for `flagstone-cracked` without a seam, so both tiles have exactly the same outermost ring of pixels. In a 4×4 repeat no single feature should draw the eye in every cell. Light comes from the upper left.
Make exactly these two frames. This brief is complete: do not ask me to confirm it. Decide anything it leaves open and list those decisions in your final report.

criteria.text: Exactly the frames flagstone and flagstone-cracked.
At most 8 colours in each tile.
PixelForge's tile seam evidence (doubled edge lines, value steps across the wrap) flags neither tile.
Both tiles share their outermost ring of pixels.
A 4×4 repeat reads as a mossy flagstone floor, with no feature that repeats as a visible pattern.
The cracked slab reads as cracked and sits in a floor of plain tiles without drawing attention to the tile grid.
